title: Duke Dougal - My 30 year quest to find a lost Roguelike
speaker: Duke Dougal
summary: Duke Dougal tells the story of searching for decades for Wilderness, a 1979 BASIC game he and his brother Paul played at their Australian high school on a Sorcerer (Z80) computer bought by their science teacher. After years of forum posts and collecting vintage computers, he bought a Sorcerer with floppy disks locally, had it repaired, and found the game file. He demos Wilderness (overworld map, random monsters, identification, levelling, scrolls, and a Hunt the Wumpus-like room-based underworld) and a Commodore 64 remake he and Paul wrote in 1984 and preserved via a magazine printout. The original author remains unknown; the source is on GitHub.

insights.claim: Wilderness, a 1979 BASIC game for the Exidy Sorcerer, already had many roguelike features: spells and scrolls, treasure, wandering a wilderness, random monster encounters, levelling and hit points.
insights.detail: Dougal played it at high school in Australia on a computer the science teacher bought with his own money. He describes it as everything you would recognise as a roguelike.
insights.quote: Wilderness was one of the games and was everything you would recognize to be a Roguelike

insights.claim: Dougal recovered Wilderness only by buying an original Sorcerer with disks after about 15 years of collecting vintage computers, then repairing it and writing a file-transfer program to extract the file.
insights.detail: Forum posts went unanswered for years. When he powered on the bought machine its 40-year-old capacitors failed, so it had to be repaired before he found a file called wilder.dos on a disk.
insights.quote: I started collecting vintage computers and did it for 15 years with no sign of one turning up

insights.claim: Wilderness is played with typed commands: advance to repaint a small map of trees around the player, identify a monster, attack, and view experience tables or a full monster list.
insights.detail: In the demo, an F on the map is a monster identified as bats; killing one levels the player up. A U marks an entrance to the underworld. Dougal selects beginner mode because it is brutally difficult as roguelikes go.
insights.quote: As you advance through the Wilderness, you can see other things appear on the map

insights.claim: Wilderness's underworld resembles Hunt the Wumpus: the player moves between numbered rooms and checks each for monsters, using scrolls to deal with groups.
insights.detail: In the demo a room holds four big worms, and Dougal reads a scroll that kills four 'greeblies'.
insights.quote: the underworld in wilderness is a strange thing because it is very much like the old game hunt the whompers

insights.claim: A 1984 Commodore 64 version of Wilderness by the Dougal brothers survived because it was printed in a magazine and Dougal kept a copy, which he retyped and debugged for 2020.
insights.detail: Paul wrote it, with Duke helping, for their home C64. The original author of the 1979 Wilderness remains unknown; nothing in the source indicates who wrote it, and the source is on GitHub.
insights.quote: It was preserved because I sent a printout who printed it in a magazine and I kept a copy for all of the years
